title: Bonds
blurb: A loan you can hold on paper: what it pays, what can go wrong, and why its price moves.
t1.title: A bond is a loan
t1.hook: Ravi's uncle lends {face} to the City Water Company. In return it gives him a certificate promising yearly payments, and his money back in {years} years. Your mission: learn to read that certificate.
t1.define: A **bond** is a loan that you give to a company or to the government. The borrower is the **issuer**. The **face value** is the amount it promises to pay back.
t1.analogy: It is like a neighbour's loan, written on paper. You could even hand that paper to someone else.
q1.prompt: When you buy a bond, what are you?
q1.hint: Read the first definition again. Who is giving the money?
q1.explain: You give the money, so you are the lender. The issuer is the borrower.
q2.prompt: What is the face value of a bond?
q2.opt.a: The amount the issuer promises to pay back at the end
q2.opt.b: The price of the paper certificate
q2.hint: It is in the definition above. It is what the loan itself is for.
q2.explain: Face value is the amount the issuer promises to pay back when the bond ends.
t2.title: Coupon and maturity
t2.define: The **coupon** is the yearly interest, as a percentage of the face value. **Maturity** is the date the bond ends and the face value is paid back.
t2.steps.3: At maturity, after {years} years, it also pays back the {face}
t2.explore: Open the lab. Change the coupon and the years to maturity. The last bar includes the face value.
q3.prompt: In the lab, set the coupon to {c6}. How much interest does the bond pay each year? Type a number in rupees.
q3.hint: Read interest each year under the bars.
q4.prompt: Now set the years to {y2}. What is the total received over the whole bond, including the face value? Type a number in rupees.
q4.hint: Read the total under the bars. It adds every bar.
q4.explain: {pay6} a year for {y2} years, plus the {face} at the end, makes {total2}.
q5.opt.a: The issuer pays back the face value
q5.opt.d: The holder becomes an owner of the company
q5.hint: Look at the last bar in the lab.
q5.explain: At maturity the bond ends and the issuer pays back the face value.
t3.title: Who can fail to pay
t3.define: **Credit risk** is the chance that the issuer cannot pay. If the issuer fails, a bond holder may get back only part of the face value.
t3.issuers: Governments and companies both issue bonds. Governments are usually seen as less likely to fail, so their bonds usually pay less. Neither kind is free of risk.
t3.mistake: Many people think a bond cannot lose money. It can. The issuer may fail, or you may have to sell early at a lower price.
q6.prompt: Which statement about bonds is correct?
q6.opt.a: A bond can lose money if the issuer fails or you sell early at a lower price
q6.opt.b: A bond can never lose money
q6.opt.c: Company bonds are always safer than government bonds
q6.opt.d: A bond pays a different coupon every day
q6.fb.b: A bond is a promise, and promises can break. Even a strong issuer can fail, and a price can fall if you sell early.
q6.hint: Reread the card about credit risk.
q6.explain: A bond is a promise. If the issuer fails or you sell early, you can lose money.
q7.prompt: A bond has a face value of {face}. The issuer fails and pays back only {rec30} of the face value. How many rupees does the holder lose? Type a number.
q7.hint: Work out the part that is not paid back.
q7.explain: Only {rec30} of {face} comes back, so the loss is {loss30}.
t4.title: Why a bond's price moves
t4.define: A bond can be sold before it ends. Its price depends on what new bonds pay. If new bonds pay more, older bonds with lower coupons are worth less.
t4.steps.2: New bonds start paying a higher rate
t4.steps.3: A buyer would rather have a new bond, so they pay less for yours
t4.explore: Open the lab. Change the rate paid by new bonds and watch the price of this bond.
q8.prompt: New bonds now pay 9%. Your bond pays 7%. Compared with its face value, a buyer will pay…
q8.hint: A buyer can get 9% elsewhere. Why would they pay full price for 7%?
q8.explain: Buyers can earn more on a new bond, so they pay less for one that pays 7%.
q9.prompt: In the lab, set the rate on new bonds to {m9}. What is this bond's price? Type a number in rupees.
q9.hint: Read the price a buyer would pay. Typing it to the nearest rupee is fine.
q9.explain: With new bonds paying {m9}, this bond is worth about {price9}, below its {face} face value.
q10.prompt: Now new bonds pay only 5%. Compared with its face value, this 7% bond is worth…
q10.hint: Try 5% in the lab. Is the 7% coupon now more or less attractive?
q10.explain: A 7% coupon beats new bonds paying 5%, so buyers pay more for it.
t5.title: Challenge
t5.recap: A bond pays interest each year and the face value at the end. It carries credit risk, and its price moves when interest rates move.
q11.prompt: Challenge: a bond has a face value of {face}, a coupon of {coupon} and {years} years to run. Add every payment. How many rupees in total? Type a number.
q11.hint: Three yearly interest payments, plus the face value once at the end.
q11.explain: {pay} a year for {years} years, plus {face} at the end, makes {total3}.
glossary.bond.def: A loan you give to a company or the government.
glossary.issuer.def: The company or government that borrows through a bond.
glossary.face_value.def: The amount a bond promises to pay back at the end.
glossary.coupon.def: The yearly interest a bond pays, as a percentage of face value.
glossary.maturity.def: The date a bond ends and the face value is repaid.
glossary.credit_risk.def: The chance that the borrower cannot pay what was promised.
